en: May Dhūrjaṭi bestow happiness upon you—he who bears upon his neck the splendor of the Kālakūṭa poison, its formidable luster resembling a beautiful garland of clusters of blue water-lilies, appearing as if darkened by the smoke rising from incense consumed as an offering. 1.
May Dhūrjaṭi, Śaṅkara, bestow and grant upon you happiness and supreme blessings. Of what nature is he?
He who is beautiful with a lovely garland made of clusters of *kuvalaya* blue lotuses.
Wearing upon his neck a beauty such as that of a garland of flowers— namely, the Kālakūṭa poison of fierce appearance and intense luster— he,
out of compassion for his devotees during the times of offerings and worship, [bestows grace].
The figure of speech (utprekṣā) is that [the sky] was made dark by that very yellow smoke of incense.

Now, the second meaning: May Dhūrjaṭi bestow—that is, accomplish—auspicious (*sukhāni*) pleasures, which are capable of fulfilling his own purpose and do not deviate toward sense objects; that is, may he bring about his own senses. Of what nature is he? Those who, upon the earth-circle (*kuvalaye*),...
"Stabakas" refers to those who praise; he is the "dāmā," the giver, of their desired object of delight.

Regarding the word "stabaka," one should observe the following etymology: that which praises is "stavaḥ," ending in a vowel (an ajanta); "stavakaḥ" is simply "stava" with the suffix *ka* added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Thus the derivation is to be understood.
What kind of splendor of the throat?
It is the burning power of the peak of those two: Kāma, the enemy of the Śṛṅgārin-s (those who imitate [the god of love]), and Kāla, who possesses a formidable and terrifying luster.

The yellowish-brown incense offered near her necklace— which was darkened by the smoke arising from the heat of the fire emitted by the serpents in the necklace— rendered it soiled, as if by that very smoke.
By this, the word-play and other such devices to be described hereafter are indicated by implication.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Oṃ! May there be well-being for all creatures. Oṃ.
Salutations to the Lord of the Gaṇas, who stands in the form of a hero born upon the marshy banks of creation, and to whom the Creator has offered obeisance.
Oṃ, homage to the remover of obstacles!
Homage to the one who takes away the warding off of obstacles, to the one who seizes the lord of serpents, and to the one who carries across the difficult ocean of worldly existence.
Oṃ! For here, at the commencement of the entire work, it is necessary to invoke one's own chosen deity; thus, in order to observe the practice of the virtuous, [the author]...

One should bow to some deity who manifests as a mental state, unstained by the affliction of the fear of non-duality; for the sake of pacifying obstacles, one should worship even Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva, thinking, "He is my deity."
The poet proclaims: "The beauty of his throat," and so forth.
May Dhūrjaṭi, Śaṅkara, grant you happiness and supreme blessings; may he bestow them upon you. Of what nature is he?

Bearing the splendor of his neck, which possesses a variegated luster and intense radiance comparable to a beautiful and charming garland made of clusters of *kuvalaya* flowers and bunches of blue lotuses, and which holds the *kālakūṭa* poison; thus he is described.

And for this reason, during the offerings at the times of worship, because she is compassionate toward her devotees, she is as if soiled by the very smoke of incense with which she is pleased; such is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā). Now, the second meaning:

May the form of Hari—Dhūrjaṭi, Śaṅkara—purify you: his mouth opened wide with a yawn, his reflection entering within the mirror of his own nails, filled with heavy wrath, causing the destruction of the enemy host, and bringing to completion the slaying of the arrogant Daityas. 2.
He who has generated a deliberation—a multifaceted inquiry—among the enemy hosts due to his terrifying form, such that their very appearance and other characteristics cannot be determined;
he who, transgressing the conduct of the virtuous, brought about the execution of the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu. //2//

May the lotus-throne, its circle of calyxes formed by rows of petals white at their edges, purify you—throne that bears the grace of Mount Meru encircled by the surging spray of waves from the Ocean of Milk. 3.

May that pericarp— the wheel of the bud— of the lotus-seat of Brahmā, who is seated upon the lotus-throne, purify you. It possesses a playful similarity to Mount Meru, which is encircled by a mass of radiance, a splashing spray, and a shimmering glow.
The petals are like the waves; the pericarp is like the mountain. //3//

On the lofty peak of Mount Mandara, whose surface is washed by the waters of the celestial river and which possesses the luster of the rising sun, there is a city named Jyotsnāvatī—the sole ornament of the three worlds—like the crescent moon upon the head of the bull-bannered god Śiva. 4.
On the peak of Mount Mandara there is a city named Jyotsnāvatī;
the present tense is used because it exists eternally, as indicated by the verse beginning with "āliṅganāditya" and ending with "yāsti. They flow.

It is like [the expressions] "vanitāḥ" (women) or "īśvaraḥ asti" (there is a lord). [The term] "surasaridgaṅgā" (the celestial river Gaṅgā) [is used] because of its similarity in color to the luster of the new sun; or alternatively, because of its similarity to new, world-surpassing trees called *arka*, or to crystals (*sphaṭika*).
Where there is splendor (*ruk*), as the crescent moon is upon the head of Śarva;
and even the head of the bull-bannered god, being washed by the waters of the Gaṅgā,
possesses a luster like that of the risen sun— due to the tawny color of his matted locks (*jaṭā*).
Śaśāṅkalekhā was also Jyotsnāvatī and Sakaumudikā; the rest is the same. 4.

In those nights, the sky—with its crescent moon situated in the center of a radiance like that of a house of fresh rubies—shone like the chest of the lord of the asuras, mangled by the claws of the Man-Lion and dripping with streaks of blood. (5)
And [the sky] was reddened by the radiance of a palace made of rubies, yet possessed a crescent moon situated in its center;
here, the word "line" (*lekhā*) is an indication for a half-moon, because at night it is impossible for there to be a mere sliver [of the moon] in the middle of the sky.
"The sky, split by the claws of Narasiṃha and smeared with blood, is like the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu,

split by the claws of Narasiṃha and smeared with blood"— here, the word *iva* ("like") is displaced [from its usual position at the end of the comparison]. By means of *iva*, [the simile is established]."

If it is argued that a change in word order is improper because the formation of a compound is mandatory— according to the rule "a compound [is formed] with non-elision of the case-ending and the original accent of the preceding member"— it is not so; for a compound must occur only when there is semantic connection (*sāmarthya*).

Furthermore, the particle *eva* is not heard immediately after the word *bhinna*; therefore, it lacks the capacity [to form a compound] because of the absence of grammatical connection (*anvaya*). If this were the case, since its employment would follow immediately after the word *vakṣas*, it would result in a compound with that [word], due to its association with that very [word].
And because the dissolution of the compound is excluded by the explicit statement in the section on "eternal" (nitya) compounds, one might object:

"In that case, since this sentence pertains to Vedic meter (*chandas*), there is no fault. If it is asked, "If the term 'Vedic meter' were not mentioned there, how could we determine that it pertains to that domain?"—the answer is: it certainly does.
The linguistic usage of the venerable author of the Bhāṣya is based on that very determination;
for he cited there examples pertaining to meter, such as "like a maiden" and "like two garments."
Furthermore, in other worldly usages, he employed the word *iva* as if its order were inverted;
for example, in the expression *siṃhīrūpam iva*, the intended meaning is *siṃhīva rūpam* ("a form like a lioness"), and not *rūpam iva siṃhī* ("a lioness like a form"). As for that which...

One might say: "This is a Vedic usage, for such is seen even in the Vedas"; according to that view, let it be observed that in the Vedas there is always the perception of *samāsa* (compound) and the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member.
How could the displacement of the word "iva" (like) be considered logically consistent? In common usage, however, there is no fault whatsoever. Enough of this loquacity! //5//
In that city, the milky ocean of the courtyard— filled with horses as bright as *jyotīrasa* gems and possessing waves of abundant, lofty rays of light—
seems to shimmer incessantly at the sight of the moon-like faces of the women stationed at the windows.
Where the houses and courtyards shine and gleam with crystals—the *jyotīrasa* gems—as if they were a milky ocean surging with waves in the form of shimmering rays;
here there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*): "as if [the light arose] from beholding the orb of the moon-like faces of the young brides. For he who...
When he beholds the face of a woman, which is like the moon and consists of the wonder of consciousness, he attains a state of exaltation;
and the sight of the lunar orb is the cause of the surging of the ocean of milk.

And in that city, the women bore cheeks moist with thick drops of perspiration from their amorous play, upon which the filaments from the flowers of their attached ear-ornaments had fallen; they appeared as if covered by the downy feathers of the shafts of the arrows of Love.
Kesara is the filaments of a flower. //7//

In that city, the moon shines forth, its rays passing through the lattice-windows, quickly reviving with its beams the God of Love— who, though long since consumed by the fire of the wrath of the Moon-crested Lord for disturbing his meditative absorption within the hearts of women— by means of its cool touch.

The "network-path" (jālamārga) is the path through the window-lattices. And because he by whom the network-path was supported with his hands was a magician (aindrajālika), he appears as if raising up something even though it has been burnt; and here, "hands" (karāḥ) refers to the palms (pāṇayaḥ).
"Net" (jāla) means a pretext (vyāja), a path (mārga), a course (saraṇi), a stream (srotas), or conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
"Raising up" (utthāpana) means restoration to life (pratyujjīvana). // 8 //
In that [city], during acts of love, the slender-bodied woman— possessing the beauty of broad and full rounded hips and a row of shimmering teeth—
would emit sweet sounds when her limbs were touched by the tips of her lover’s fingernails, like the female tortoise of the Flower-Bowed God.
The *nitamba* is the region of the hips; it is also called *prasthikā*. The *daśana*s are the teeth; they are also called *kolamba*s.
The *kūrmī*, *trisarikā*, and *sairandhrī* are well-known names for a particular type of lute (*vīṇāviśeṣa*). [This refers to] the beloved's...

*Avamarśa* refers to tearing with the tips—the edge portions—of the husband's nails; and it is also the beloved’s highly desired rubbing with the tip that remains fixed as a plectrum for playing [the lute].
Where the palace of Bāṇāsura, built of sapphire, shines with large ruby windows situated on both sides,
as if his body were drenched in streaks of blood from the wounds at the roots of his arms severed by Viṣṇu’s discus.
"Both sides" means on both flanks;
the word *ubhaya* has the same meaning as the word *ubha*, but it occurs only in compound (*vṛtti*). "Blood-born" means blood.

There, the breezes— cooled by following the ripples of the celestial river flowing nearby— enter through the lattice windows of the ruby palaces and dispel the exhaustion born of lovemaking among the women.
*Abhyarṇam* means proximity or vicinity. // 11 //
In that city, during the nights, the white crescent moon appeared like a branded mark upon the cheeks of beautiful women;
it resembled the surface of a clear crystal fragment held in the hand of the God of Love, which was streaked with calluses from the striking of his bowstring.
Where the crescent moon, reflected upon the cheeks of the brides, shone white; yet, being marked— that is, accompanied by its spot—
it was like a clear crystal gem resembling the surface of the forearm, variegated by the scars of [the bowstring’s] cord.
Nyāsa is entrusting. 12.

Upon which the hosts of gods suspected the Milky Ocean had approached out of eagerness to behold the moon upon Śaṅkara’s crest; and which, under the guise of a mass of radiant ramparts reaching the sky and built of bricks of light, resembled the ocean itself. 13.
A rampart (*vapra*) is a wall built and constructed from bricks made of *jyotīrasa* (a type of precious stone) and from lumps of earth fashioned into squares;
[the short vowel in *iṣṭakā* is used here] according to the rule *iṣṭakeṣīkāmālānāṃ citatūlabhāriṣu*. A "resemblance" (*nibha*) is a pretext (*vyāja*). // 13 //

Lakṣmī did not abandon that palace, which was filled with women who were like female swans on Lake Mānasa with their radiant and graceful movements, and who, adorned with jeweled anklets, sounded like the cymbals of the fish-bannered god of love.

The *jhallaryas*—specific types of musical instruments belonging to the one whose banner is a fish (*jhaṣaketana*), the one whose standard is a sea-monster (*makaradhvaja*)—also produce a tinkling sound (*jhāṃkārin*) similar to that of anklets (*nūpura*). // 14 //

In those nights, the circle of the moon’s rays, mottled by the smoke of beautiful aloe-wood incense, attains a beauty as if marked with scars from being caught in the clamps of the silver door-panels of the latticed windows. 15.
Because it was mingled with the smoke from the burning of aloe-wood incense, the circle of moonbeams— the orb of the moon’s rays—

was pressed against the two panels of the window-shutters that served as its cover, which were being joined together. Through the friction of these two panels being closed, [the moonlight appeared as if crushed].
It bears a beauty as if marked by a scar; this is because a scar is black. // 15 //
The bedchamber was strewn with fragments of petals from blooming blue lotuses that had served as ear-ornaments, crushed during the friction of amorous play;
they lay there like shattered shards of the sword of the Flower-Armed God (Kāmadeva) as he tore through his beloved.
"Women," thus he praises. 16.
From the openings of the windows, the smoke-sticks of playful black aloe-wood incense streamed forth,
like the hands of darkness with flickering, long-fingered flames, as if fearing the touch of the nearby moonbeams.

Those which are close to the rays of the moon—the "staves of smoke" belonging to darkness, appearing like hands, with fingers that are flickering and long-tufted; or rather, fingers whose tips (śikhā) are long—such are they. 17.

That city shone with the women of the capital, who were like creepers on the wish-fulfilling trees; they possessed the fresh sprouts of youth, charming yet devoid of self-awareness due to their transformation through the persistence of passion, and resembled the grove-paths of the Golden Mountain. 18.
Those women who possess a continuous attachment to passion, and who are likewise devoid of the affliction— that is,
the obstruction— of the state of transformation, namely old age;
[this refers to] their delightful and fresh youth.

Those whose "pallavas" (sprouts) are their "prasaras" (expansions); in the other sense, those which possess an "anubandha" (continuity) of "rāga" (redness), and which are devoid of the "avamarśa" (touch/contact) of the state of "pariṇāma" (ripening/maturity)— that is, the state of full development— such are the leaves of fresh youth, unaging and untarnished.
"By whom"—by those women. "A grove-path" is a path thick with trees. "Puraṃdhris" are principal women. // 18 //

There, rows of jewel-encrusted palaces reaching toward the clouds bear a splendor in every direction through their doors— which, though closed, appear as if they were opened wide from afar by their spokes fashioned from bands of beryl— during the nights.
Those whose door-panels and shutters were joined together; appearing as if their mouths were bound;
having become visible even at night; and reaching the sky, pervading the heavens. 19.
In that city, even though the moon-crested Lord Śiva dwells there constantly, the God of Love resides fearlessly within the bodies of the city’s matrons;
for they provide him protection by mounting their thousand-fold bows—their eyebrows—and discharging the arrows of their side-long glances.

In the enemy of Smara, whose crest-jewel is the moon—here, "in the body" (*dehe*) is used in the singular to denote the class, meaning "in bodies. His side-glances alone are the arrows; his eyebrows alone are the bows, the *śarāsana*. // 20 //

In whose nights the water-lilies do not grow poor upon the pleasure-ponds; white as a mass of dense, shimmering moonbeams by their radiance, they bear a resemblance to the ivory tusks of the elephant of Love. 21.
Manmatha himself is the elephant;
there, the lotuses—even when closed—bear a resemblance to its tusks, for they do not lack luster, nor do they diminish in beauty. And in this case, the excellence of the location is the cause.
Or, because of the rule "bibhranti" and "of the neuter," the augment *num* is applied. //21//
Where, for a moment, the ruby archway— by the radiance of the bodies of the sun’s horses hanging nearby on its pole—
shines as if it were adorned with garlands of greeting made of green sprouts.
The *kūbarī* is the chariot; the *kūbara*, however, is the pole that supports the yoke (*yugandhara*). A *vandanamālā* is a garland made of leaves and flowers. // 22 //

In this city, the circle of watchtowers and palaces, kissed by the orb of the sun, mimics the playful appearance of a vast water-trough for the overflowing cascade of nectar—the spreading radiance of the beauty of the young women’s moon-like faces. (23)
Beauty accompanied by loveliness is indeed a stream of nectar.
An *aṭṭāla* is a defensive position on top [of a wall] used for combat.
A *sāla* primarily consisting of such [positions] is the city rampart.
Because it has the form of a bracelet, it imitates a basin for watering plants. // 23 //
The deer-eyed women, whose beautiful forms are delightful with the crescent moons of their limbs made manifest, steal the heart;
there, they are the radiant smiles of the temple of the Flower-Armed God (Kāma), accompanied by the unfolding of sweet, charming, and clever gestures and emotions. 24.
Where deer-eyed women, with their limbs made manifest and their bodies revealed, enchant the heart with forms as beautiful as the crescent moon;
such is that bodiless one, the flower-weaponed god of love, who follows after their gestures and expressions.

A *saudha* is a white palace; they are those for whom laughter is the object of repose. A *hāva* is a particular kind of gesture arising from the limbs of sexual passion (*ratyaṅga*). And it has been said:
"That wherein the movements of the eyes, eyebrows, and so forth, indicate the form of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*)."
That is to be known as *grīvārocaka* (the stiff-necked), a *hāva* arising from the limbs of love.
Thus, *bhāva* is desire. 24.

In that city, within the lotus-pools of the mansions, the clusters of lotuses—whose interiors were streaked with the luster of ruby stairways—shone with the brilliance of the sun; they seemed like the rays of the moon held captive by their beloved for his pleasure.
*Niketa* means a house. A crystal that is red due to the influence of its substrate is called *lauhitīka*;
the suffix *-īka* is applied after *karka* and *lohita*.
[This is] for the beloved of the sun, whose radiance is not dull.
"I have come to report this desired matter: that by your grace, we, having acquired greatness, have seized and brought back our enemies.
In some versions, the reading is "aśītaruci" (the cool-rayed moon).
In this regard, it should be understood that the rays of the moon were captured by the sun in order to bestow benefit upon those very [rays] which are dear to him. // 25 //
In that city, the golden flagstaffs set upon the divine temples, inlaid with fragments of rubies, shine forth with their intensely rosy luster,
as if embraced by streaks of lightning flashing from the edges of clouds torn apart at their very peaks.
"Inlaid with pieces of rubies" means studded or covered; that is to say, accompanied by brilliance. "Of golden banners" refers to the flags made of gold. // 26 //
In that very deep night, as he proceeds to his beloved’s house with a hand-lotus holding a blooming lotus for sport,
the world of women stands by, as if having been given a supporting hand by the impetuous darkness of the evening.

*Adhiniśīthinī* means "during the night. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of a case ending (*vibhaktyartha*). *Vaibhāravam* is a modification (*vikāra*) of the night (*vibhāvarī*); here, the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed in the sense of a modification, as in *naiśam*. However, when expressing abstract states (*bhāva*) and so forth, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule *kālāt ṭhañ*.
Only the suffix -ṭhañ shall be applied. 27.

In that city, the beautiful sound of water-machines in the pleasure-lakes, possessing the splendor of the *kaiśika* and *madhyama* scales following their sequence, is heard by the flocks of domestic swans as they stretch their necks and still their feet, shaking their wings. (28)
A pleasure grove is a garden. A *tāmarasinī* is a lotus pond. He by whom the splendor of the *kaiśika-madhyama*, a particular type of song, was constantly and continuously mastered;
that is, they have constantly heard the *madhyama* [scale] even in other regions.

They perceive that very sound as being similar to it—[the sound] with its neck craned, its feet motionless, and its wings fluttering. This is called *svabhāvokti* (description of the essential nature), characterized by the specific qualities of genus and action. //28//

There, on the banks of the palace lotus-pools, flocks of swans—darkened by the radiance of rays from emerald gems—captivate the heart; they appear like the darkening essence of the moss that has long been consumed there as it transforms.

*Aśmagarbha* is emerald; *harinmaṇi* is a synonym for it. It has undergone transformation, has matured, and has entered into the limbs. Having been enjoyed for a long time, for many periods, it has been fully absorbed. // 29 //
In that city, at night, the clusters of stars in every direction— whose bellies were licked by the rays from the palaces constructed of emeralds—
embraced the beauty of the multitude of dewdrops clinging to the tips of freshly sprouted, tender *kuśa* grass-blades.

A *harmya* is an excellent mansion. *Pratidiśam* means in every direction; the suffix *ṭac* is applied here because it belongs to the group beginning with *śarat* in the category of *avyayībhāva* compounds. *Udabindavaḥ* refers to drops of water.
In the phrase beginning with "manthaudana," there is the substitution of "uda" for the word "udaka."

In that city, the moon, its brilliance eclipsed by the faces of women overflowing with loveliness, bears a state of turbidity in its heart; thus, during the nights, it seems to enter the depths of the underworld under the guise of its reflection upon the jeweled pavements. (31)

Wherein the moon, because its radiance has been eclipsed, enters as if into another subterranean realm; the sense is that this is due to shame. "Turbidity" refers to the dullness caused by a stain and despondency. "Heart" means the center and the mind. // 31 //

At dawn, the streets there shine, strewn with heaps of jewel-like flowers scattered upon the floors of the inner apartments; they appear variegated like masses of stars being cast down by the impact of the rising rays of the sun.
"Cast out from the surface of the pavement" means discarded because of its uselessness.
"Karas" refers to rays; it also means the hand. This is because [the object] is fit for falling upon that striking.

She shone, having assumed a posture fashioned with the care of an embrace by her husband; she bore a girdle of the rays of the jewel-stars that shifted about, while her broad hips were like spreading *sāla* trees and her waist was marked by the lines of a blooming moat.
(Thus ends the description of the city: It was fashioned by the sound of the *muraja* drums, which were like the embraces belonging to her husband, the Lord.
That particular mode of standing shone forth;
they say that here, among the various types of covered instruments, the *tripuṣkara* is the foremost.
Among them are two known as the *aṅka* and the *kāliṅgyaka*, and another named the *ūrdhva*.

And since she is perceived as the heroine (nāyikā), another interpretation may also be applied: that her state is such that she remains pervaded by the funeral pyre (citā) due to the intensity of her longing for the embrace of her beloved husband. // 33 //
Desiring to show grace to the worlds, the Lord— having assumed a constructed body for that purpose and having destroyed the circle of his enemies—
inhabited that palace white as a temple, appearing like the King of Serpents with the cool-rayed moon as his crown.
A "body of transformation" (*nirmāṇadeha*) is a body fashioned by will, delimited by space, time, and so forth;
he is one by whom that [body] has been assumed. He is one by whom the circle (*cakra*)—meaning the multitude—of enemies has been destroyed;
and he is one whose [discus] Sudarśana has likewise destroyed the circle of enemies.

In that view, "ari" refers to a sharp spike (tīkṣṇakīla) joined with that; it is white like a palace because of its palaces (saudhaiḥ). In the reading "kalāvacūla," *avacūla* means a decorative mark (*cihna*).

The foreheads of the multitude of those who have taken refuge in him bear the scars from prostrating at the lotus-throne of his feet; these scars appear as if they were the pupils of bright eyes fixed upward upon his body, which is about to become Rudra. 35.
"Prapannāḥ" means those who have come under [her] control. "Rudrībhaviṣyati" is a locative singular form (saptamyantam) qualifying her body (vapuṣaḥ). // 35 //

The fire of his arrows was instantly fanned by the wind of the hissing serpent, who— distressed by the pain of his tightly bound topknot— emitted flames that flickered with fierce rays as if to provide assistance while burning down the three cities.
"Sāhāyakam" means assistance in the burning of Tripura; [the suffix] *vuñ* is applied according to the rule "yopadhāt". "Pṛṣatkaḥ" means an arrow. // 36 //

First there arose the submarine fire, ignited by the hissing of the multitude of serpent hoods that served as the bowstring for the Mandara mountain dancing within his ears; then followed his arrow, matted with a mass of blazing flames, which consumed the three cities.
The *tāṇḍavita* is drawn; the bow [is bent]. // 37 //
Upon his head, the Mandākinī shines, its mass of waves shattered by their friction against the crown-jewel and the skull-ornament;
it possesses the beauty of a cool, nectarous cascade flowing from the crescent moon leaped upon by the fire of his upward-turned eye.

Whose throat, having gazed upon the Gaṅgā—polluted by the persistence of jealousy because she was forcibly embraced by him under the pretext of the dark hue of the manifest *kālakūṭa* poison during their playful tussle of hair-pulling—shines as if it were being embraced by the Yamunā herself. (39)
"Defiled by the persistence of envy" is an adverbial modifier for the action of "observing. // 39 //
The sky of that [Lord], as if desiring to ascend, shines forth under the influence of a persistent anger born from jealousy toward the daughter of the Snowy Mountain;
it appears like the Gaṅgā flowing toward her path, emerging from the portion of the jewel in his matted locks which is pressed by the serpent upon his crown. 40.
Envy (*abhyasūyā*) is the inability to endure the virtues of others. Envy as a persistent state of anger is a longing for what belongs to another.
A turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) is a head-wrapping. "Facing the path" (*pratipatha*) refers to heaven, as if it were directly before one due to the onset of rage. (40)
By him, who was laughing as he shook off his head out of fear of being crushed— leaving behind only the face of the sun who had sought refuge—
the row of teeth was seen falling downward like a line of ancient skulls slipping from the binding of a crown.
Pūṣan is the Sun; that which remains as the residue of his mouth, which is left over from the western quarter, is seen as one who has come for refuge. From the skull-caps, the wrist-joint has fallen.

The fragment of the moon, whose beauty and splendor had been effortlessly surpassed by the lotus-face of the Daughter of the Mountain King, was long borne in [Śiva’s] hand like a captive child, its mass of hair loosened as it slipped from the knot at the tip of his matted locks. 42.

The moon, fallen from its bond, was for a moment [or long] held by his hand so that it might not roll upon the surface of the earth; a fragment of the moon was playfully captured and restrained like a small child. And of such a one...
Is it proper for the child to be held by the hand out of affection, or out of fear of fleeing?

Even today, upon whose head the skull of Brahmā attains a splendor resembling the unceasing sound of the Vedas, as it issues from the deep cavities of its interior being filled to the brim with the waters of the Mandākinī. 43.
"Eti gacchati" means "he goes"; "aśāntā" is the word division; [it refers to] Parameṣṭhin, that is, Brahmā.

In the grand displays of his *tāṇḍava* dance at the onset of the night of universal destruction, the lords of the mountains, struck by the winds from his staff-like arms, retreat before him one after another, as if merely to provide space for the play of his circumambulation. (44)
*Tāṇḍava* is an exuberant dance; *ḍambara* is ostentation or elaboration;
*parikrama* is the movement of the feet. // 44 //

The moon attains the splendor of a ruby foot-ornament shattered by the sharp edges of the mountains cast down, as its primary streaks are formed by the circle of the tips of his ankles and feet raised with the impetuous speed of his imitation.
On whose ankle is joined the first line of the circle—
meaning the moon, which possesses such a primary circular line or the first digit of the orb, [placed] upon the head by the pouring of the stream.
It attains the splendor of an anklet made of a ruby gem that is being shattered;
"anukāra" means dancing.
A "daṇḍapāda" is a foot raised upwards in the shape of a staff. // 45 //

In his dances, the mountains—uprooted by the wind from his staff-like arms, their foundations on the surface of the earth shattered by the play of his various movements—wander through the very path of the sky as if terrified of falling into the netherworld. 46.

*Ucchalitāḥ* means tossed upward; *paryastāḥ* means overturned. *Cārī* refers to the form of movement performed with one foot; *nṛttavicchittayaḥ* (variations of dance) include *samapāda*, *atipāda*, and so forth.
That which is the movement of a single foot is designated as *cārī*.
That which is the stepping with the two feet is called *karaṇa*.
The sky is space. 46.

Night, approaching her beloved moon—whose brilliance is fixed upon his crown—climbs gracefully toward his lofty neck, appearing like the dark shadow of the Kālakūṭa poison, its body as black as a cloud at the time of universal dissolution; she seems to circumambulate him. 47.

The metaphorical identification (rūpaka) expressed in the phrase "the night is like the shadow of the Kālakūṭa [poison]" is such that the location where the crown (kirīṭa) is placed is the very place of the radiance (dhāman) of the head (mauli), which stands above. // 47 //

He bears a white skull upon his throbbing head, its hair-tuft like a digit of the moon nestled within the cavity of a face flickering like a wave of the Gaṅgā, possessing the beauty of a swan with its tip of a lotus stalk barely grasped by its indistinct beak. 48.
Kapilā is indeed Kālī. 48.

The serpent of his necklace, its eyes closed as if in imitation of him whose eyes were shut in the meditative absorption of twilight, narrowed its timid gaze in fear, overwhelmed by the mass of ash-dust smeared upon it from his ritual smearing. (49)
*Uddhūlanam* is smearing with ashes; *kūṇitam* means contracted. // 49 //

There is no room for me here in this heart, which has been flooded by the nectar of love centered upon the Daughter of the Mountain King; for it was here that the flood of poison, whose flames were like the fires of the three worlds now kindled, fixed its mark with the words "He who has a neck too long. (50)
Because this heart of mine is filled with the nectar of love, there is no room or space for [the poison] here. Furthermore, in the presence of nectar, there is no scope or movement for poison.
It has been kindled—that is, it has been inflamed. //50//

Seated in the middle of his body as he drew back his flowery bow until it reached his ear, the god of love—reduced to a mass of yellowish powder by the pollen of the flowers—appeared as if already enveloped by the flames of the fire of wrath, even before any transformation of his mental state had occurred. 51.
The syntactical connection is that [the mind] is likewise prior to even the transformation of the mental fluctuations; "parīta" means pervaded. // 51 //
When the bow was drawn by the Flower-Armed One (Kāma), who had shattered his intense meditative absorption with a frown upon his brow,
the upward-turned eyes of the enraged Lord closed like buds, as he was being overwhelmed by the impetuous force born of that agitation.

The third eye of him [Śiva] closed due to his wrath; it contracted to bring forth fire. The *vibhaṅga* is the breaking or the manifestation of the frown (*bhṛkuṭī*). There was a disturbance or friction of that bow. // 52 //

He whom the gods, terrified, beheld before them as the body of the Flower-Arrowed One underwent its terrible transformation from the intensity of the burning—seeming to scatter the Kālakūṭa poison from the hollow of his throat under the guise of the smoke from the unrestrained fire of his *huṃ* sounds. (53)

"Vikiran" means spreading or expanding. This is a form of *apahnuti* (concealment), wherein it is denied that "this is not the Kālakūṭa poison, but rather the smoke from the fire produced by the sound 'huṃ'. // 53 //
When his meditative absorption was broken by anger, the mass of flames from his upward-glancing eyes became fuel for the God of Love;
thus, Makaraketu found his footing in the very side-long glances of graceful women, adorned with the play of their eyebrows.
*Laḍita* means radiant or shimmering; *laṭabhā* means charming or captivating. // 54 //

The face of him who, assuming the illusory form of a Kirāta, was gazing at Arjuna with wrathful eyes—its complexion deep crimson—appeared as if it were the transformation of the mass of flames from the fire of the eye fixed upon his radiant forehead. 55.
A mass of flames is a collection of flames; its transformation is its ripening. "From afar" means from nearby. // 55 //

His eyes longed intensely to behold the Daughter of the Mountain, whose form was exceedingly beautiful, with the feathers of peacocks adorning her ears like ear-ornaments and the tips of her breasts embraced by garlands of gunja berries. 56.
*Patatrakhaṇḍa* means the cutting off of wings; *guñjā* means a *raktikā*.
He desired [to drink] up to the very throat with water. 56.

The mind of him who had assumed the form of a Kirāta was deeply pierced by the piercing glances of the daughter of the mountain as she became a Śabarī—glances whose long, darting pupils possessed the beautiful luster of peacock feathers worn as ear-ornaments. (57)
It is pierced and struck down. The peacock is the *kekī*. The two eyes are the two arrows, which are like stakes (*śaṅku*) covered with peacock feathers. 57.

As the Kirāta’s body leaned against him, a multitude of sweat-drops suddenly sprang from his forehead—its surface bristling with spray—as if to conceal the heat of his eyes; Arjuna wiped them away with his hand.
Arjuna is the wearer of the crown; by whom the quarters were pervaded with sprays [of water], such was he who, with his hand,
[held] from his forehead that mass of sweat-drops born of Arjuna’s anger.
*kṣiptaḥ* is derived from *kṣip*, meaning "to throw. By the rule *ṛcchatṛchatyṝtām*, there is *guṇa* substitution [of *i* for the root vowel]. // 58 //

He, by the grace of his face being slightly bent in play, beheld the crescent moon of the crest-jewel resting upon the surface of his breast; it bore the charm of a jar of nectar that had been surpassed by the waves of the churned Ocean of Milk. 59.
In one half [of her body], there is a breast, upon which is reflected the crescent moon of her crest-jewel. 59.

By whom his chest—vast as the rock of the Himalayas—was made to bear the lotus-hands placed upon the surface of the breasts of the Daughter of the Mountain King, appearing during the graceful movements of his dance as if the lute were resting there along with its gourd. 60.
Because Gaurī was standing in front at the time of playing the lute, even when the reading is *kāṇḍavīṇā*, the meaning is exactly this same one. // 60 //
He who, after a long time, casts off his handful of twilight water with his slender body bristling with horripilation and covered in beads of perspiration,
his beauty of gaze now fixed and motionless by the joy of beholding the moon-like face of the Daughter of the Mountain resting upon half of his own body.
The sight of the moon-like orb of the Daughter of the Mountain’s face [was obtained] because it was reflected in the handful of water. // 61 //

As if out of impatience, his eye emerged from the forehead of the Lord who is half-woman, desiring to examine whether or not a union would truly occur between these two halves of a body that had been joined together.
From whose eye the pupil darted forth with speed, as if desiring to begin an examination of that alliance.
The rays of the nails on the two branches of whose feet—feet upon which Rudra’s gaze does not rest too intently—are brightened in their foreparts;
they possess the beauty of pale-rooted, reddish-pink lotus petals, yet are tinged with the orange hue of a flame.
The space before him was illuminated by the rays from the nails of the toes of his pair of feet,
as well as by the flames of fire.
The tawny eyes of the Rudras, intent on prostration, bear the beauty of a lotus with a white root.
With mouths made resonant by hymns of praise, with jeweled ear-ornaments slipping from their ears, and with fruitful twilight rituals made beautiful by the worship of his steady feet,
the throngs of Siddhas, Sādhyas, and gods attended upon him every day.
Their radiant crowns were embraced by the tips of their outstretched hands. // 64 //
The hosts of immortals, bearing the names of those already perfected and those yet to be perfected, attended upon that god;
they served him with worship of his feet that was beautiful and captivating, and for this very reason, their twilight devotions were fruitful and not in vain.
At the conclusion of each canto, this great poem was composed by a poet who diligently employed the "jewel-word" (ratnapada) marked with his own name.
Thus ends the first canto in the *Haravijayaviṣamapadoddyota*, the work of Alaka, son of the royal sage Jayānaka.
Then, once, out of a sense of playful delight, he—
whose hand was sportively grasped by the daughter of the Snowy Mountain—
ascended a mountain peak whose configuration was graced by fresh golden creepers.
He adorned the pleasure-pavilion of Aśvadhāman. // 1 //
Having entered a pleasure-house on the ridge of the city of Aśvadhāman, that god adorned it and caused it to shine. // 1 //
When he had accepted the seat and was skilled in discourse anointed with sentiments favorable to the Daughter of the Mountain King,
the lords of the immortals approached him, their golden armlets having their gem-encrustations crushed by mutual friction.
Upon that mountain peak, a mass of rock on the Himavat, smeared— that is, anointed—
with mercury (rasa), these lords of the gods, the sovereigns of the immortals, beheld it from afar. This group of fifteen verses forms a *kulaka*.

From nearby, they beheld him bearing the celestial river [Gaṅgā]: its mass of matted locks was like a creeping vine of moss; the curved crescent moon on his crest was like a broad lotus stalk; and the skull-ornaments were like laughing swans. // 3 //
She whose mossy creeper is the circle of matted locks, and whose laughter is the swan that is the skull-cup. //3//

He bears upon his head the celestial river, which has been emptied of its waters by the masses of sparks from the fire emerging from eyes struck by the wind from the hissing breath of hooded serpents coiled as ear-ornaments, yet which is gazed upon with satisfaction by Gaurī.
A venomous serpent was fashioned and attached to his ear for the purpose of an earring;
sparks were the feathers of his crest;
[the city] was emptied and thinned by the heaps of those [sparks]; [this was done] by me, who am thoroughly pleased.
[She is] the one who has been beheld. // 4 //
The solar disc on the surface of his radiant forehead was suddenly entered from nearby by the dull-rayed moon, which had reached a state of attenuation upon reaching the crest of his hair.
He bore [the form] as if it were being occupied, with his eyes turned upwards. // 5 //
"Being occupied" means being brought face-to-face. The poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is expressed by the phrase "as if desiring to enter. [The moon] has already attained it;
the cold-rayed moon, the maker of frost, [seeks] the solar orb again for the sake of complete satisfaction.
The solar disc enters the sky of the eye-socket (or the sky of the eye-cavity), because it bears that very form; the vault of heaven is not the [external] sky. //5//
"How is it that even a mere crescent of the moon-like face of the Daughter of the Mountain is not equal to the full moon?"— thus thinking sorrowfully,
as if a flame arising from his upturned eyes were about to fly upward, he gazed.
It rests upon the vicinity of the high, elevated surface of the forehead.
"Lekhāpi" means: by the moon (śaśin), as if desiring to fall, [the mark] was placed near my forehead. // 6 //
In one place, his severed head shone with a crown and skull-fragment, its brilliance made crimson by the sprinkling of blood dripping from the skin of his elephant hide,
as if adorned by a row of teeth reddened by the tint of betel.
*Stamberama*s are elephants; *kṣataja* is blood. // 7 //

Having placed upon his crown the moon—which, with its splendor of moonlight, makes the sky pure and acts as a beloved lover—the [Lord] wears, under the guise of the shadow of the thick Kālakūṭa poison, the luster of that [moon’s] spot clinging to his broad neck. 8.
He was making the stainless sky his garment by means of the splendor of the moonlight; he was delightful, acting as a lover; [I saw] the mark of that moon. 8.
She holds the seven worlds devoured by the jaws of time, dark as a cloud heavy with the burden of the ocean,
bearing a line of poison whose brilliance is like the glow of a yellow incense-stick revolving within her throat.
The wick is a support made of cotton for the flame. // 9 //
He bears the ocean whose circling waves are curved by the hoods of the lordly serpents, which serve as the spokes for the thousand whirling, fierce jeweled conchs;
and he carries the abode of the tortoise, which is illuminated by the mass of radiance from the peak of the formidable and vast Kālakūṭa poison resting upon his throat.
"Maṇi-śaṅkha" is a *dvandva* compound meaning "jewels and conch-shells," or it refers to "fragments" or "parts" of jewels. "Bhaṅgura" means crooked or curved.
"Viśaṅkaṭa" means broad or extensive. [The suffixes] *-śālac* and *-śaṅkaṭac* are applied after the word *vi*.
The peak is a lofty heap; the mass of radiance itself is the tortoise-dwelling ocean. 10.

White with ashes as his body-unguent, with the crests of his shoulders crowded by serpents possessing the luster of the peacock feathers of cuckoos, he possessed a splendor resembling the ocean whose waves are like milk, their ripples darkened by the smoke of the submarine fire. 11.
*Parapuṣṭa* means the cuckoo (*kokila*). Its *picchā* is its plumage or bundle of feathers. *Kūṭa* means a peak or summit. *Ūrmimālā* means the ocean. // 11 //
He shone brilliantly, for his high shoulder-tops were struck by the breaths of the serpents upon his armlets, causing fresh ashes from his smearing to rise upward;
these ashes reached the moon’s orb above, which was spinning with its whirlpools, and thus attained a resemblance to it.
"Keyūrārtham" means for the sake of an armlet; "pannaga" means a serpent; "sāvartacakram" is an adverbial modifier describing the specific nature of the whirling motion. 12.

He bore a chest as broad as a slab of the snowy mountain, adorned with a necklace of serpent-hoods that appeared darkened by the radiance issuing from the black poison (kālakūṭa) residing within the deep hollows of their throats, resembling a garland of blue lotuses hanging thereon.

That which is the hollow, the center, is its abode; from that [abode] emerges a luster that makes even the serpent Kālakūṭa appear excessively darkened—[the Lord] whose necklace is composed of such a serpent. 13.
He beheld the daughter of the Snowy Mountain resting upon his lap, her body beautiful with a golden-brown luster like a fragment of fine gold;
yet she appeared once more as black as soot, surrounded by the radiance from the throat of Kālakūṭa, which was darkened by the collyrium. 14.
Furthermore, she is Kālī, the Black One; for it is said that by her very nature Śailakanyā possessed a dark body, but through the power of her asceticism,
she attained a fair-complexioned form which became the basis for her designation as Gaurī.
With this intention, there is a repetition here. 14.
Fanned repeatedly, resting his head upon the pillow of his hump with his two long, upraised arms folded across it, he was served by the bull from afar—
its tail-tuft acting as a chowrie— with winds from its formidable crest, as if the animal’s mind were filled with devotion.
The grammatical construction is as follows: "being fanned by the Maruts—the winds—acting as instruments, with the humped [bull]. The humped one is the bull of Hara (Śiva). // 15 //
His pair of feet is rendered fragrant by the *pārijātaka* flowers from the ear-ornaments of the hosts of gods who have come to serve him;
it bears the mark of the reflections of bees following the scent [of those flowers], while his multitude of moon-like nails possess a clear interior. 16.
It was made fragrant by those lords of the hosts of immortals, Indra and the others, who had come for the sake of service and whose ears were adorned with *pārijāta* flowers serving as ear-ornaments;
[it was made fragrant] by their very nails.
His pair of feet, bearing the marks of the moon, was distinguished by their preeminent rays.

[He saw] the one possessing the form of an elephant-faced [deity], whose shadow of throat-poison was dispelled by the luster of his teeth, who was in close proximity, and who seemed to be placing upon his face streaks of thick Chinese powder-dust like the radiance of the fire from his upward-gazing eyes. (17) [This is part of a *kulaka* group of verses.
"The one possessing the form of an elephant-faced [deity]" (*karivaktramūrti*) means that his form (*mūrti*) has the face of an elephant (*karivaktra*).
Cīnapiṣṭa is vermilion. // 17 //

Having prostrated before him, whose golden footstool resounded with the strikes from the tips of the crests of the jeweled crowns [of the sages], and when they had been presented by Śailādi with their heads bowed, they were comforted by occupying their appropriate seats. 18.
Śailādi, the son of the sage Śilāda, is Nandin;
by him the drums, such as the *āṅkika* and others, were struck—that is, beaten.
A *viṭaṅka* is an elevated place; its very edge is the *ṭaṅka*, meaning a chisel or a sharp tool.
Resounding, meaning making a sound. // 18 //

The drums were struck in succession, clearly marked by the *ārjā* rhythm, delightful through their specific tonal qualities, diverse paths of movement, varied tempos, hand-beats, and rhythmic cycles; they displayed distinct methods of percussion and were accompanied by the various *karaṇa* gestures. (A pair of verses) Then the drums were struck, manifesting an array of distinct paths, diverse movements, tempos, hand-beats, and rhythmic cycles.
They established the rules for sweeping, the application of yoga, the classification of paths, the captivating of the mind, and the methods for various musical instruments.
Those drums upon which the placement [of notes] has been specifically determined during the process of tuning by means of the scales beginning with Ṣaḍja; as it is said:
"Gāndhāra should be applied to the left [head], and Ṣaḍja to the right head."
The fifth [note] is indeed in the Ūrdhvaka; these are remembered as the notes of the mārdaṅga drums.
And so forth. *Mārga* and the others are the methods of striking and breaking [the drum] for the player. Among them, *mārga* is as follows:
when the drums were struck mercilessly by Nandīśa and their skins resounded with deep tones, Taṇḍu divided [the beats].
Then, amidst the *āsārita* movements, he performed the *tāṇḍava* dance, which was rendered beautiful by the full array of its seven imagined variations. // 20 //
The attendant named Taṇḍu sang toward him the song called Tāṇḍava, which he himself had composed;
"puṣkara" means the mouth, and it was divided into two types: the *sukumāra* (delicate) and the *āviddha* (elaborate).

In the three types of *āsārita*—the superior, middling, and inferior, as previously mentioned—the seven varieties known as *āvāpa*, *udvāpa*, *niṣkrāma*, *vikṣepa*, *praveśa*, *śamana*, and *saṃnipāta* have been conceptualized; it is exceedingly beautiful because of these. [The phrase] "in the *āsāritas* such as *abhisṛta*" refers to the seven varieties (or, with the variant reading, the three varieties).
Some read: "therein, *abhisṛtam*, *parisṛtam*, and *pariveditam*";
these three, beginning with *abhisṛtam*, [are the variants]. However, that reading appears inconsistent with the *Bharata*.
In that regard, this is because their various subdivisions have not been stated. //20//

The Mothers, who bear the Daughter of the Mountain in their embrace, whose crests are adorned by the moon-crested Lord, and whose eyes perceive the aesthetic moods (*rasa*) and emotions (*bhāva*), performed that dance— charming with the movement of an elaborate display of graceful gestures, the very ornament of play.
The Mothers are Brāhmī and the others;
their dance is that in which the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī) is embraced—that is, placed in the midst—by them.
"Maula" means primary. "Apadāna" refers to auspicious conduct; it is a hymn concerning that [conduct] in which such praise is found.
The "rasa-vision" refers to [the goddesses] such as Kāntā;
the "bhāva-vision" refers to [the goddesses] such as Snigdhā; and the "rasas" refer to the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others.
These [rasas] possess complexions such as dark-blue (*śyāma*), and so forth, as it has been said:
The erotic sentiment is declared to be dark, while the comic is said to be white;
the pathetic is pigeon-colored (grey), and the furious is proclaimed to be red.
And so forth. //21//
With bodies as fair as the *kundam* flower—neither yellow, nor pale-red, nor white—the lords of the Gaṇas wandered about, abiding in the graceful movements of their dance;
they were like the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) incarnate upon a prepared stage, engaged in the performance of dramatic gestures.

Those by which the stage-platform (*raṅgapīṭha*) is adorned and decorated; in the reading *raṅgaśīrṣāḥ*, it means the head of the stage (*raṅgasya śīrṣam*), that is, the head-platform (*śiraḥpīṭham*). This is according to [the rule] beginning with *aci śīrṣaḥ*.

If it is argued that because the substitution of *śīrṣan* for *śiras* is prescribed only when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) follows, its use here— where no such derivative occurs— is not justified,
this is not so; for [the rule] "after *śiras*, when preceded by the negative particle, in the *vrīhyādi* group" applies.

It has been concluded from the recitation that there exists a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *akāra* which is the word *śīrṣan*; for it is not the case that the substitution of *śīrṣan* is to be prescribed by that [stem] in connection with a suffix, since that [substitution] applies before a vowel (*aci*).

Since this is already established by the word *śīrṣa* itself, the formulation of the suffix rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*), namely that the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* apply only after the negative particle *nañ* followed by *śīrṣa*, etc. // 22 //
As the Enemy of the Cities himself rose up before them with impetuous zeal to instruct them in the performance of his own perilous dance,
the surface of the netherworld became strewn with fragments of the jewels from the hoods of Śeṣa, crushed by the level ground beneath his feet.

"Ujjihāna" means rising up; "avakīrṇa" means mixed or intermingled. "Puraripu" refers to Śambhu (Śiva). "Viṣamaprayoga" refers to a composition that is charming despite its complexity or mixture. // 23 //
Having arisen, he threw the world into turmoil— a world from which the swans had fled due to the clearly visible darkness—
and which was drenched by the gloomy rain of spray from the waters of the ocean tossing against the tips of his mane-like matted locks of smoke, like the Divine Boar at play.
The world (*bhuvana*) is the triple-world (*tribhuvana*) and water (*jala*). (These are either confused, intermingled, or uplifted. The *haṃsa* is the sun and a bird.
The *sindhu* is the Gaṅgā and the ocean. And in a stormy day, there is manifest darkness.
The swans, the birds, dissolve away. // 24 //
As his arms, white with the ash-salve applied as unguent, stained the sky with the whirling movements of his sword,
the crested peacocks fled in terror, mistaking them for rows of white clouds, their bodies with tails gathered into clusters.
The movements of the fingers are the gestures (*abhinaya*),
known as *āveṣṭita* (contracted), *udveṣṭita* (extended), *vyāvartita* (turned away), and *parivartita* (turned around).
These are fourfold, distinguished as bodily (*aṅgika*), vocal (*vācika*), attributive (*āhārya*), and internal (*sāttvika*).
As he was being groomed, the peacocks—whose bodies were covered by the tails of the birds held up by his hand—fled in all directions.

The peaks of that mountain, whose far side had its masses of darkness crushed by the glow from the rays of the hoods of the serpents upon his firm arms, were instantly pulverized by the trees of his arms, which served as a boundary for the sun’s rays.

The mountain Lokāloka is the limit of the rays of the sun; it is that whose opposite side possesses ground from which the mass of darkness has been driven far away. [There,] they were crushed—that is, reduced to powder. // 26 //
As he laughed, his multitude of arms flung out in all directions, and his head shook through the sequence of his *aṅgahāra* gestures,
the celestial river— its waters flowing over the peaks— assumed the graceful beauty of a shimmering curtain of fine Chinese silk.
The *aṅgahāras*, such as the *sthirahasta* and others, are accomplished through thirty-two specific *karaṇas*.
The *karaṇas*,
in turn, are combinations of the *mātṛkās* which produce *cārīs*, *sthānakas*, and *nṛttahastas*.
And those [offerings], such as the handfuls of flowers and so forth, number one hundred and eight. And it is said: "Whatever places and whatever noble ones... (27)
As if wishing to dance before her, the fire of her eyes quickly turned the peripheries of the quarters of the sky tawny;
its movement constrained by the rim of the sun’s orb, it dispelled the curtain of the royal parasol with its rays.

The very sunlight served as a curtain; he cast it away before him with the flames of his eye, having dispelled it by means of his splendors. [In the verb *asyat*, the augment *thuk* is added, resulting in *asthuk*. 28.

As if for the purpose of displaying a continuous series of various dramatic gestures being performed before him from every direction, he created mountain peaks crushed by his clearly extended and restless staff-like arms as he traversed the paths. (29)

"Being drawn forth" (ākṣipyamāṇaḥ) means being introduced. "Recaka" means whirling; its "impulse" (rayaḥ) is that [whirling]. And that [impulse] is of four types, according to whether it involves the hands, feet, hips, or neck. Here, the "recaka of the hands" (hastarecaka) is intended, because it is only possible within the movement of the arms.
He is the Lord. 29.
With their arms raised high and thick, white with the ashes used as body-unguent and with hands moving in the graceful gestures of dance,
they resembled a milky ocean filled with thousands of masses of waves formidable with swirling eddies.
Dancing hand-gestures (*nṛttahasta*), a whirlpool (*āvarta*) is the swirling of waters; resemblance (*pratirūpatā*) is similarity (*sādṛśya*). // 30 //

As he performs his dancing movements, his thousand hands— with palms as red as blooming *japā* flowers— act as the mass of petals for this world-lotus, which has the vast golden mountain [Meru] as its seed-vessel and the circle of the earth as its pericarp.
The word *tala* is not feminine when it denotes the lower part or one's own form;
*varāṭikā* means the seed-vessel;
and *aravinda* is indeed the world. Within that [world] belongs this *harasya*.
With their hands, they acted as if they were a mass of leaves; that is, they assumed the state of being a mass of leaves because they remained in that form. //31//

He bore a crescent moon that had slipped from its loosened position on his crown due to the shaking of his head, appearing as if it had approached to follow the shadow of the *kālakūṭa* poison in his throat because it was joined to his thick, rounded shoulders.
"Ghaṭita" means joined or met; "vidhuti" means trembling; "bibharāmbabhūve" means was borne or maintained. And the moon is invariably a follower of the night. // 32 //
For a long time, before him— whose upward-turned gaze was possessed of rays and whose tawny luster had faded away—
the fragments of his lotus-hands appeared, with their clusters of petals that were the spreading, formidable, and blood-red fingers, due to the manner in which they were held in a continuous circle.
The sun is Marīcimān; the movements are the dramatic gestures (abhinaya). // 33 //
For a moment, the waves of the Milky Ocean, tossed by the force of the wind from his tree-like arms smeared with white ash-dust,
spread through the sky like the celestial Gaṅgā embracing vast, rising billows of clouds.

Because they were smeared with the coating of ashes, the wave-breaks of the Ocean of Milk were rendered doubtful— made objects of uncertainty as to whether they might be the tree-like arms of that Blessed One.
In the sky, the waves—both the ripples and the yearnings—spread out and swirled due to being struck by the wind; [there was also] the celestial Gaṅgā, the Ganges of the heavens.
As if longing to see their kinsmen who had gone to the subterranean abodes of Pātāla, the hooded serpents spread out their coils;
with the winds from the hissing breaths emitted by their circles of hoods, they dispersed the waters of the oceans that were bound within their jeweled necklaces. 35.
The *maṇibandhana* is the junction between the hand and the forearm; those by whom [the weapons] were bound—that is, fixed—in that place, they discharged them, meaning they made them strike. // 35 //
With his circle of arms being displayed through the sequence of distinct *aṅgahāras* and *karaṇas*,
the Moon-crested Lord bore a splendor resembling Mount Kailāsa and the Kalpa-tree shaken by the winds of universal destruction.
The *aṅgahāras* and *karaṇas* are those previously mentioned; such was that Mount Kailāsa, whose wish-fulfilling trees were trembling. // 36 //
By means of those brilliant lines of ash-particles from his waving staff-like arms, he seemed to perform an even more intense composition,
as if laying out the preliminary measurements for the intermediate spaces of the worlds, suitable for the exertion of his own dancing that was about to burst forth.
"Nirbhitsyamāna" means that which is about to be broken open; "yogya" is a word formed with the suffix *yat*, meaning that which is capable of yoga. // 37 //
The sky became like a surface inscribed with the tips of rays emitted from the ends of his fingers as he began his dance,
appearing as if marked by the spots of many thousands of shimmering, curved moon-buds.
Crooked means curved. A mark (aṅka) is a sign. // 38 //

Then, urged by the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices (Indra), the Seasons—whose forms were the personified splendors of their own domains—sought refuge with him who had previously served them and whose mind was now gratified, for he had been devastated by the humiliation inflicted by the demon Andhaka. //1//
The disturbances,
the agitations,
serve you.
Thus,
the definition,
its essence.
Holding with their hands various clusters of flower-stalks that offered swarms of bees attracted by their intense fragrance, they knelt upon the ground, having been presented with humility by Nandin.
(with humility),
with propriety.
*Nikāraḥ* means contempt or humiliation;
*abhirāddham* means pleased or propitiated;
*upadā* refers to a gift or an offering.
Then, having prostrated before him, they— whose crests were adorned with bees rising from the golden slabs as they moved about—
occupied the jeweled stone seats placed nearby by his permission.
Then he [performed] this [movement],
and then this [movement],
with a leaping motion that was unerring.
Then the Lord of the World, his sprout-like lips bathed by the cascades of rays from his teeth, spoke these beneficial words to them as they were stumbling in their rising.
With a voice as deep and majestic as the thundering of clouds sluggish from the heavy burden of fresh rainwater. // 4 //
Why have you, who are so full of vigor, suddenly fallen into a state of emptiness as if the worlds themselves were undergoing a reversal?
Now it is your very complexions that, turning grey, speak of the pain of a thorn in your hearts. 5.
They have gone;
the powerful ones have gone.
O Śalya, [the power] of the mighty,
the craft.
Mukha means face; sukha means happiness;
akāṇḍe means at an improper time.
"Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) means lack of essence.
"Full of vigor" (*śuṣmiṇaḥ*) and "radiant" (*tejasvinaḥ*) are vocatives addressed to the seasons. "Dart" (*śalyam*) means suffering.
"Grayish" (*dhūsarāḥ*) means soiled. //5//

While the Lord of the Maruts—whose arms were exceedingly radiant with the flashing thunderbolt and as thick as the coils of the King of Serpents—stood there, why did the son of Diti yawn, desiring to bring calamity upon the worlds? 6.
*Kuliśā* and *Kulaśā* are the Lord of the Maruts, the Sovereign of the Gods.
Exultation has been manifested; arrogance has been revealed. // 6 //

Risen from the lotus-seated Brahmā—who is as tender as the core of a lotus root and possesses faultless wings—the world-lotus bud has blossomed; surely you alone are capable of protecting it, like bees. (7)
Bisakanda,
[I wish] to drink from the seat that is tender with nectar.
Brahmā, whose seat is the lotus, protects; "kamalāsana" means that his seat (āsana) is the lotus (kamala),
[and thus] he is indeed the lotus itself.
The seat is his support; his followers are his wings and feathers;
the world itself is the calyx and pericarp of the lotus.
To drink, to protect, and to taste. // 7 //

Like the poetic creation of Brahmā concerning the realm of manifestation, clear, wonderful, and possessing vividly unfolding narratives, your pure fame is being spread far and wide by you all, surpassing even the glory composed by the Ancient Poet (Vālmīki). 8.
This world, the domain of creation and the object of the emanation of Druhiṇa— that is, Brahmā— is like a poem.
By you speaking thus, fame is spread abroad because of the manifestation of your skill;
however, in poetry, "sargas" are divisions consisting of sections.
"Citrā" means various kinds; it also refers to "citra" (pictorial) compositions such as *cakrabandha* (wheel-arrangements) and the like. "Vṛttayaḥ" means linguistic usages or styles;
in another sense, they refer to the types of alliteration (*anuprāsa*), namely the urban (*nāgarika*) and the rustic (*grāmya*).
The poet is also Prajāpati.
Then, having uttered these words to the Earth— whose voice was as steady as a rain-cloud— the Primal Being,
awakened by the glance of Śeṣa, the foremost of the pure ones, who beholds the characteristics of the entire circle of seasons, slowly [arose].
The earth, though not possessing stability,
appears as if it were stable.
Having emerged from the soundless [state],
from the sounding.
Having swallowed [the words], he uttered speech that made his face resonant with a continuous humming sound, its beauty of fragrance enjoyed by hovering bees;
it was as if he were vomiting forth before him his own store of flowers, made formidable by the filaments of the rays from his teeth. 10.
The face,
emitting honey.
With his eyes narrowed by the impact of the flames arising from that [fire] which destroys the friend of Smara,
he seemed for a moment to harbor resentment toward the third eye of the moon-crested Lord Śiva. 11.

As if his words were being carried before him by the sweet warbling of bees—who had approached out of a longing for the spray-like drops of nectar from fresh mango blossoms clinging to the tips of their ears—he spoke thus: "It is honey. 12.
(cakkalakam) The group of four beginning with "sthitavatī" [is as follows]:
*gām* means speech.
The summer is scorching;
love alone is one's kinsman when it brings about that destruction.
As if his heart were filled with envy at the upward movement of Hara’s [tears], he closed his eyes; "śīkarakaṇāḥ" refers to tiny droplets.
"Previously," that is, before;
"as if in a speech being taken away," we ourselves, your followers, inform you.
The intention is that it is not proper for the Lord himself to speak [thus] in our presence. (9–12)

For you, O Lord, who preside over the lotus-throne of the heart, the sole witness to the affairs of the three worlds, whose consciousness is entirely devoid of the absence of resentment—what is there that is not known to you? (13)
He presides over it;
he presides over the seat.
The threefold sacrificial grass, the threefold [oblation].
What indeed exists, and what does not exist?
There is an obstacle, a hindering cause; by means of the impairment or affliction caused by that [obstacle].

For you, whose consciousness (*saṃvit*) and cognition (*vijñāna*) are devoid [of duality] and who reside within the heart-lotus, there is nothing here that is unknown; for you are omniscient. Therefore:
Who indeed could be a witness for you, who are already the witness to the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of the world?

The word *viṣṭara* means a seat. The genitive case [in *tava*] is used according to the rule "the sixth [case ending] is used after a word ending in a *kta* suffix when it denotes the present time. (Pāṇini 2.3.67) // 13 //

O Sinless One, your fourfold innate nature—consciousness and the rest—is renowned in the world as being such that nothing else whatsoever possesses even a fraction of its excellence, which attains a supremacy surpassing all others. (14)
Non-cognition and so forth are innate; cognition and so forth are innate; cognition and so forth are innate;
cognition and so forth.
Your fourfold set of qualities— consisting of consciousness, sovereignty, dispassion, and dharma— is celebrated in such a way that it has attained its most eminent state.
There is nothing else superior to this that possesses a further degree of excellence.
Of this very [state]:
Because it possesses excellence; the genitive case in "asya" (of this) is used in the sense of disregard. //14//

O Lord, for you who perceive the further shore and whose radiance is the unimpeded consciousness of simultaneous perfection, the knowledge of the true nature of the entire circle of objects—attained through the conventions of words—never occurs anywhere. 15.
The true nature (*satattva*) and the nature of cognition (*matattva*)— the true nature of the entire range of objects is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and one who knows that is [the knower].
Those [entities], having arrived through the convention of words,
do not attain the state of being produced by means of a word or a linguistic convention.

This is not tenable; for others understand even that which is beyond the senses, such as the *apūrva* and so forth, solely through the medium of words. But the Lord, moreover, possesses the light of unimpeded knowledge even regarding Brahman.
One who sees the further shore perceives everything directly, without depending on scripture; "the further" (para) means the most excellent, that is to say, Brahman. // 15 //

O Lord, just as the light of the sun, shining without distinction, expands its radiance upon all things, so too does your intellect—unobstructed, stainless, and free from the darkness of delusion—manifest its presence. 16.
It expands;
when it has expanded,
it is stainless.
The term *nirmalīsamā* means "equal" in its non-distinctive operation;
*vibhā* means "radiance. // 16 //
O Lord, although we have already comprehended the full extent of all things that exist, you ask us this today;
therefore, it causes us to gather a supreme store of merit now, for the moment of your sweet conversation with one another is most delightful. (17)
The term *yuta* here means a multitude or collection (*vistaraḥ samūhaḥ*); extension (*prathana*) is not intended in this context.
Since the root *prath* is used in the sense of "expansion" (*prathana*) and not in the sense of "sound" (*śabda*), the suffix *ghañ* does not apply. // 17 //

Having attained a state of being distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti) and devoid of modification, and being inactive with respect to the qualities inherent in prohibited objects—you alone, indeed, are the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth principle, as declared by the explicit words of the Cūlikā Upaniṣad. 18.
The subjects for the sage named Pañcaśikha, the son of Cūluka, are as follows:
existence, unity, purposefulness, subservience to another, distinctness, and cessation;
conjunction, disjunction, the plurality of spirits, the persistence of the body, and the final state of existence.

Thus, there are ten categories. By means of their words, you alone are declared to be the twenty-fifth principle (puruṣa) and are explained in its entirety. You are designated by etymological derivation as "puruṣa" because of your dwelling (uṣita) within the city (puri), that is, the body.
Some maintain that the "crest-ornament" (cūlikā) topics concern subtle matters:
primordial nature (prakṛti) is the unmanifest cause,
while the transformations (vikṛtayaḥ), such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, are of a different character from it.
As it has been said:
"Root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both natures and modifications;
the group of sixteen is only a modification; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor modification."

Thus, because it is eternal, the properties inherent in things are denied: namely, the six modifications of being— being born, existing, transforming, increasing, decreasing, and perishing— and that which is of such a nature is also devoid of activity.
Because of indifference. //18//

Devoid of the nature of the well-known manifold of worldly pleasures, and unable to accomplish even the slightest thing anywhere, you have descended to a state where the functions of the senses are void; oh, how truly like Prakṛti you are, O lover! 19.
"Aha! How extraordinary that you, O lover of Prakṛti, are so well-matched to her! For the man’s state of being a lover consists in the desire, 'May I enjoy Prakṛti.
His suitability, however, is here rejected through irony by means of the figure of *viparītalakṣaṇā* (contradictory indication)."

For thus, the person (puruṣa) is celebrated as being devoid of that "rasa"—meaning passion, emotion, or state of being—by which one attains expansion; he is incapable of performing even the slightest action because of his lack of activity (niṣkriyatva). He is "without body" (avapura), meaning his essential nature is unmanifest.

It is devoid of the activity of the thirteenfold instrument—the sense organs such as the eye—which consists in the grasping of objects; moreover, since primordial nature (*prakṛti*) has a form dissimilar to this, how can there be a similarity between these two? This is also true for that which [consists of] aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), such as the erotic and so forth, and emotional state (*bhāva*).

Devoid of the many kinds of qualities such as *sattva* and the like, and due to a deficiency of wealth, unable to accomplish even the slightest task, and being "bodiless" (*a-vapuḥ*)— meaning lacking physical form— he was [endowed] with the *karaṇa* well-known in the treatises on erotics, such as *utphulla* and so forth, and with his mode of livelihood (*vṛtti*).
It is truly strange that this man, who is destitute of any means of acquiring wealth, should desire some particular woman. 19.

O Protector, those who rely upon the ten causes, whose minds are purified and free from all disturbances, and who follow the distinctions of the mature Sāṃkhya doctrine, declare that for the accomplished ones, that supreme state is indeed non-return (*anivṛtti*). (20)
The learned followers of the Sāṃkhya, who abide by the specific doctrine of the great seer Kapila, the elder of the Sāṃkhyas,
do not [attain] that supreme state of yours which is transcendent and from which there is no return.
Furthermore, cessation is that from which the return to saṃsāra occurs; they establish such [a cause] through ten reasons known as *vīta* and *avīta*. Among them:
"Because of the transformation of differences, because of homogeneity, because of activity from power," and so forth.
Because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the manifold world.

The five reasons presented as proofs for *prakṛti*—namely, that "the unmanifest is the cause"—are *vīta* [syllogisms]. An equal number of those same reasons serve as proofs for the *puruṣa*, and these are *avīta* [syllogisms]. They are as follows:

The Puruṣa exists because the aggregate is for the sake of another, because there must be a reversal of the three guṇas and so forth, because there must be a presiding controller, because there is the state of being an enjoyer, and because of the activity for the sake of isolation (kaivalya).
Thus, those by whom the nihilistic doctrine—which is a perversion—has been set aside on the basis of this [teaching], are for that very reason pure of heart. //20//

Bestowing upon you—a knower of the reality of all objects who is exempt from the experience of the fruits of karma—the status of being a supreme person, the wise establish the word "Īśvara" as referring exclusively to you and no other. 21.
There is no other object [of such power] such that,
having acted in this way while you bear the state of being a distinguished person, the wise designate you by the name "Lord" (īśvara) with respect to both auspicious and inauspicious karma.

The fruit, which consists of pleasure and pain, is a ripening that is devoid of its experience because there is no aspiration for it; and because one who perceives the reality of all objects is untouched by the latent tendencies of karma and afflictions. And it has been said:
The Lord is a distinct soul, untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or latent dispositions.

Those of pure vision have never, like other ascetics, perceived your sinless lordship—which is devoid of both positive and negative concomitance—as something merely inferred by the friction of examining the ends of firm bonds. 22.

The "limit of bondage" (*bandhakoṭi*) refers to the continuous stream of bondage consisting of *prakṛti* and so forth. By contact with that, the sovereignty of other yogis is rendered miserable, because they have previously experienced saṃsāra;
but for you, who are eternally liberated, it remains forever of one and the same nature.
It is empty of both existence and non-existence; therefore, it is faultless and, by virtue of possessing excellence, it is luminous—this the ones of great intelligence know. And it has been said:
"In that [state], the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed."
Thus:

"In former times, when the lotus-born Brahmā had become intensely heated by his asceticism as he desired to create the worlds, there arose that which possesses five characteristics and is employed in all ritual acts, such as sacrifices. (22-23)

O Blessed One, that which the Vedas declare as the supreme state, which is described as having many faces and feet, and reaching which a person is not born again— that very thing is the signifier (*vācaka*) of you, who are the syllable *praṇava*.
(Yugmam) That very *praṇava*, the syllable *oṃ*, which first arose from that same [source] for the sake of Brahmā who desired to create the worlds, is the designator of you alone.
Therefore you are addressed [as follows]: as it has been said—
"The *praṇava* is its designator"— together with that.
By means of five characteristics— namely, the constituent parts in the form of the letters *a*, *u*, *m*, the half-moon, and the bindu—
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva constitute the fivefold deity.

O Śarva, for you who have attained the sole state of being the Guru of the leaders of the gods—emptiness regarding the dharmas of cessation and arising—and who possess the power to consume all that is moving and unmoving, no one here can ever surpass you. 25.
O Smara, O Kāla, you who are perceived here through action, through sequence, through parts, through number, and through your own characteristic marks—
having tranquility as your beginning, middle, and end— you, by your own power of illusion, bring even that very Time (Kāla) to its end.
(These two form a pair:

Having attained the samādhi of Śaṅkara—which is free from vitarka, whose sphere of activity is unstable vicāra, which is devoid of the feeling of pleasure, and which is unaccompanied by asmitā—a person never again succumbs to delusion by his own will. (27)

O Lord, by the power of Your will, You obstruct even that state of discriminative vision—which, through the destruction of contrary states to the nature of the power of consciousness, has cultivated detachment toward primordial matter—even while that vision remains established. 28.
