O Lord of the Gods, yogins who have perfected their discipline within various target-mandalas such as the *tapa* and others, come to possess an unimpeded and variegated self-consciousness regarding the abodes beginning with the worlds. (29)

O Lord, by Your will, for those yogins who have transcended the triad consisting of ignorance and whose path of cessation has been brought face-to-face with their state of abiding, neither the foundation of ten million levels nor the sevenfold [foundation] arises. (30)

O Lord of the Thirty-three, for human beings whose minds are otherwise characterized by unrestrained wandering, there arise within the seats of the tongue and other senses cognitions pertaining to tastes and so forth, which are of the nature of worldly existence and serve as the foundation for an undisturbed state. (31)

The person who possesses the cognition "I am characterized by pure gold" is indeed you, O Puruṣa; from the tips of your hair down to your nails, you are said to be made of gold by the followers of the Upaniṣads, having attained a state consisting of fivefold experiences such as pleasure. 32.

O you who are white with virtue, it is you alone who are sung in this world by Brahmā as he chants the Sāman with its many paths, which possesses the excellence of the fivefold *bhakti*—beginning with the *sphya*, *hiṅkāra*, and so forth, and concluding with the *nidhana*. 33.
When those who have attained stability in the fixed sequence and tones of the Vedic revelation remain firmly established in the pursuit of the eternal,
you alone resound within the distinct objects such as the *aparāntaka* meters, characterized by the ten types of sound.

Having become the cause for the cessation of all offices of authority and having turned his back on the world of speech, this atom (jīva), desiring to know your true nature, sings of the profound *madraka* melodies; O Hara, [protect him]. 35.

O Lord, having attained the state of being the cause of eternal satisfaction—just as the drinkers of Soma regard you, the nectar—you, who are hidden in the cave of the heart, are milked by those who are devoted for the sake of the supreme vow of the sacrificial grass-strewn altar. 36.

For the skillful practitioner who is endowed with the capacity for the various divisions of Sāṃkhya, the weighty Yoga, and Dhāraṇā, and who remains seated in a firm and comfortable posture, the eightfold divine power indeed proceeds when the mind has become serene. (37)

Indeed, Sarasvatī herself, consisting of you, has appeared in a great form, endowed with the quality of excellence through notes of two kinds and four modalities according to the sequence of the Vedas, sweet with the clear sound of the *sāman* chants. 38.
Those renowned as seers of the higher and the lower, who know the ancient lore, declare that which is praised by the universe as "not this, not this.
That very supreme reality of yours, devoid of all limiting adjuncts and means of apprehension, is truly wondrous. 39.

O Blessed One, those of pure vision have declared you to be that very person—the high ground, wind, fire, water, and so forth—which, for men, is the unimpaired transformation of sensation and is composed of that [sensation]. (40)

O Blessed One, those by whom this scripture has indeed been studied here—beginning with the syllable *praṇava*, possessing the state of finality (*virāma*), and having its seven ultimate meanings explained by the Serpent (Śeṣa)—surely attain Your very station. (41)
O Lord, though devoid of feet, you move; though deprived of hands, you assume the state of a grasper;
though without eyes, you look; and though without ears, you hear everything, yet you do not know, and yet you know. 42.

Thus, O Lord, for one who beholds you—the imperishable one who bears a form unique to all the worlds and endowed with the most wonderful excellence—indeed, the entire consciousness of that virtuous person undergoes a transformation. 43.
(Yugalaka) Just as the orb of the moon reflected in a mass of water-waves is removed from a reservoir,
so too has the heat of the sun, which had taken refuge within the shelter of the tree's sprouts, fallen upon the earth. 44.

Just as the sky, though remaining one and the same, clearly assumes a manifold state when situated within mortars and other vessels due to its transition to various supports—yet remains unchanged—so too are you. (45)
(Yugalaka) Since Hari is said to possess but a single activity, while those who are portions of Him are established in three, four, or many activities,
that other manifestation of Yours, the possessor of all souls and great majesty, remains situated here. 46.

O Protector, it is indeed marvelous: he pierces the jewel with his gaze; instructed by you, he weaves it without fingers; he fastens it on even though he lacks a neck; and he worships it even though he is without a tongue. 47.

Though assuming many forms, you maintain a single form; though having attained the nature of stability, you are transitory; though situated in the sky, you do not transcend the earthly realm; and though standing in close proximity, you possess remoteness. 48.

Though beyond both consciousness and unconsciousness, He appears as if not beyond them by assuming their appearance; though beyond both being and non-being, His state is beyond both being and non-being, yet He remains devoid of many faces, feet, or limbs. (49)
Though situated within the orb of the thousand-rayed sun, the cool moon maintains a wealth of heat;
whether you are of a dual nature or perhaps neither, you are thus profoundly mysterious and truly wondrous. 50.

(Tilaka) O Blessed One! Alas, you are indeed difficult to grasp by anyone through the renown of your manifested form and majesty; nor are you accepted anywhere by any wise man, even though you are established as the very essence of suchness. 51.
O Lord of Gods, you have no going and no coming; you do not manifest anywhere, neither outside nor within.
Taking as your object the suchness that is empty of dualistic appearance, you appear only to those whose minds are not devoid of grace. 52.
Indivisible indeed, you abide as the illuminator of the entire collection of objects in the world;
yet, through the words and sentences, you have extensively attained the state of being an auxiliary to the things that are to be expressed. 53.

Although you maintain a single nature through conceptual construction, you are nevertheless grasped by people as manifold, divided by the beginningless ignorance that functions through the paths of agent, object, instrument, and so forth. 54.

That which, being without beginning, middle, or end, indeed manifests as the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*) by assuming the form of all objects—that indestructible body of yours, the reality of the word *Śiva*, the foundation of the world, they proclaim. 55.

O Lord, when the conceptual constructions of this world have not yet ceased their delusive flow, and when the two paths of worldly convention depend upon one another, the intellect and its verbal expressions attain their cessation only by reaching beyond [the limits] of their temporal boundaries.

O Bhava, you appear to no one as a profound and chaotic state of heterogeneity, which transcends both the superior and the inferior that the world relies upon, and which is rooted in the ultimate secret doctrine (upaniṣad). // 57 //

O Lord of the Gods, you—whose activity is distinct from the qualities (*guṇa*), who abide beyond the qualities, and who have taken refuge in that which is the source of nature (*prakṛti*)—have clearly attained both a state of dissimilarity and a state of similarity with the path that extends to the six limits of existence. (58)

Even though you abide beyond the range of the intellect, you are somehow discerned by those whose vision is fixed within the interior of the syllable Om (praṇava), by means of instruments that are free from limiting adjuncts and which have overturned the graspings of error. 59.

The wise, by means of the *suṣumṇā* channel, attain Your state—You who have transcended the fourth state (*turya-vṛtti*), whose existence is the healthy sustenance of all living beings, and whose self is the unsubdued subduer of worldly existence (*apavarga*). 60.

Having swiftly pierced through the four mandalas, the skillful ones entered you—who possess a form profound because it has shaken off all conceptual construction, who are unsurpassed, infallible, and marvelous, and who are unobstructed. (61)
O Lord of the Gods, the fire of the body, agitated by its own crest of flames, is struck by the mind impelled by you;
it, O Lord, stirs the fivefold vital air that is the cause of the stability of the bodies of embodied beings. (62)

Having mounted the chariot whose driver is the unobstructed mind and which has the ten external organs as its support, the atom wanders among the sense objects like the blue-throated Śiva; yet, by Your will, it turns back once again. (63)

O Blessed One, you alone are worshipped by the wise as the Guru of embodied beings who abide in the abodes of the ears and other senses of the entire host of presiding deities, yet you maintain a supportless existence within the ether of the heart.

Just as waters do not enter into a jar that is filled with dust and other impurities, so too, O Blessed One, the atoms do not enter into You—who are free from all affliction—by Your will, through pleasure and the other [feeling-states]. (65)

Sporting with the grace of revolving petals within the hollow interior of the heart-lotus, you have entered as the inner self of the entire world; thus, you bring about the various states of existence that depend upon the two paths [of liberation and worldly rebirth]. 66.

Within the solar orb of the Youthful One—the healthy self composed of the three Vedas—residing in the splendor of the *Ṛg* and shining with the radiance of the *Sāman*, you appear as the *Yajus* formulas;
though minute within that circle, you manifest as the Person (*Puruṣa*), profound with the distinctions of various appearances. 67.

Clearly, you alone, assuming various names while possessing the form of Hari, perform diverse actions for those who have taken refuge in you; bestowing day, season, solstice, year, and so forth upon the world, you alone shine as the sun with its rays. 68.

O Lord of the Gods, through yoga, the unimpeded state of embodied beings—whose bodies consist of all the atomic principles and who are mutually obstructive—is perceived by you like a triple staff (tridaṇḍa) conditioned by your own presence. 69.

O Lord, it is said that in ancient times, the deities presiding over the intellect and other faculties— Bṛhaspati and the rest— entered the minds of those who know the past, desiring not to seize the compositions of the world which are ruined by mutual disputes, but wishing instead to lead them forward.

By means of this knowledge of yours—which destroys the delusion and agitation of those who enter it, and which all knowers of the knowable have entered—it serves as the shattering of the dense bolt on the door to the path of liberation; thus, the individual soul attains the state of Śiva.

O Lord, although the origin of the worlds is without beginning or end, and although You remain as their progenitor while being Yourself devoid of birth, and although qualities and other attributes exist in You, praise based on lineage cannot truly apply to You. 72.

Because the effects consisting of dyads and so forth—which have as their object a sphere of experience utterly pure and beyond the senses of ordinary birth—are observed, the wise infer your causality, even though you are a non-agent by nature, just as a potter is the cause of a jar. // 73 //

The wise proclaim Your agency, O Lord, as being devoid of any external instigator; for You, whose nature is utterly unimpeded and who act through Your own irresistible will, are the Sovereign whose very self is free from all constraints.

This world, consisting of the three qualities, arose indeed from a mere fragment of Your power when it was intensely agitated—that power which assumes the form of the array of all-pervasive and perfect energies and is renowned for its manifold transformations of existence. 75.

O Lord of the Worlds, from you—who are free from blemish, whose power and majesty are firmly established, and whose self is distinct from the circle of bound souls (paśu) and fetters (pāśa)—proceeds here this entire sphere of existence (bhāva-maṇḍala), which possesses the nature of both the conscious and the unconscious. 76.

O All-pervading Lord, the various multitudes of objects emerged from you like flaming sparks from a fire—objects whose depths were shattered by your rays, which simultaneously rendered them unconscious and diverse in form. (77)

O Lord, although You abide in a state of wondrous and supreme majesty that has attained eternal duration, Your activities do not exhibit any contradiction regarding the sequence or simultaneity of their accomplishment in the fulfillment of all purposes. (78)
Presiding over the circle of your complete powers, you create, protect, and destroy the entire universe;
O Blessed One, you remain with a stable form composed of the five mantras, being devoid of the two types of birth.
When the state of being earth (the gross elements) is agitated, the primordial nature (prakṛti), which had entered the cave [of the heart], then rises up like a bundle of straw;
for the sake of the world's manifestation, the qualities (guṇas), though mutually dependent and previously motionless, remain fixed like the strands of a rope. // 80 //

Since you have fashioned this entire manifold circle of effects, from the dyad upwards, which encompasses all objects of experience, you are inferred by the wise as one endowed with extremely subtle vision, knowledge of all things, and omnipotence. (81)
O Sovereign Lord, through your pervasive form you bring about the proximity of all things, and through your sovereign form you accomplish every purpose;
by means of your power (*śakti*) which has attained a dual nature, you have manifested the state of all that is moving and unmoving. 82.

O Lord, by Your will, the obstruction of the expansion of Your eye—the world-flower whose radiant and manifest form is woven with unimpaired power and qualities—was never encountered anywhere at any time. 83.

The cave, situated like the hollowed-out pod of a Madhuka flower, has been made a secret chamber by you; it never undergoes any change in its state, for it is a temple where all stainless atoms are bound together by their qualities. 84.

Just as the earth, according to its capacity, brings forth a pure seed into the form of a sprout, so too, O Lord, is your desired activity here—the entire mandala of existence—brought to fruition through the performance of all inherent natures. 85.

Others, however, declare that from the imperishable *prakṛti-tattva*, whose nature is composed of the collection of renowned powers, the entire array of effects beginning with intellect (*dhiṣaṇā*) proceeds, being non-different in form from it. (86)
For what insentient object indeed can assume the status of an agent in the accomplishment of its own functional wheel?
Therefore, they declare you, the Lord, who consists of the activity of consciousness, to be the originating cause of all living beings here. 87.

Even at the time of universal dissolution, O Lord, you remain with your sovereign power undiminished, your radiant consciousness unobscured throughout all worlds; clearly, like a spider from its web of threads, you are the cause of the multitude of atoms. 88.

O Lord, others indeed declare that the Puruṣa—who is the sole cause of the world, whose nature is causeless, all-pervading, immutable, devoid of the states of the qualities (guṇas), and who has attained a state of identity with You, the Sovereign—is Your very self. (89)

Others, however, declare that the collection [of the three]—which is devoid of the world manifested by the activities of primordial matter (prakṛti), God (īśvara), or both, as well as by consciousness (cit) and so forth, and which is free from limiting adjuncts (anupādhika)—is determined by two means of valid cognition and consists of a triad. 90.

Others, who propound that liberation is natural, maintain that the birth of living beings consists solely in existence, independent of any other complete causes, and that their downfall is as sudden as the falling of a peacock's tail-feather. (91)
Others, however, know the pure essence of sound (*śabdatattva*) to be undisturbed by the fluctuations of dissolution and emergence;
for it is this that appears here as the transformation consisting of this entire circle of existents, both moving and unmoving. (92)

O Lord of the Gods, others of profound intellect, who refute objects that fall outside the three types of conceptualization—even when those are impossible within the interval between moments—maintain that the stability of the world is consciousness alone. (93)

Those whose minds are free from grasping at both [extremes] and who take their stand upon the position of the Madhyamaka view, their intellects certain of the stable reality, achieve the state of having accomplished all that was to be done, being colored by your excellence. (94)
Some, whose rays of consciousness have been made to blossom by Your grace, say that the atom is indeed supersensible;
others, however, O Lord, know that it is merely a sensory perception resulting from delusion, though they take it to be of the nature of the Self. 95.

"Consciousness is never observed here, even in the slightest degree, outside the body or anywhere else that is not its size"—thus having reached this certainty, those of perfected intellect have established the opposite of your [teaching on] eternity and omnipresence. (96)
O Blessed One, by your grace, those whose dense forest of delusion has been cleared away perceive you as one of pure vision;
yet others, such as Kaṇabhakṣa, Jaimini, and the Digambaras, proclaim you to be manifold in nature. 97.

Others, whose mental activities are bound to an unstable state by the nature of being both characterized and uncharacterized, O Blessed One, deny your existence through reasons such as non-arising, possessing nihilistic intentions. (98)

Some, whose minds had leaped forward, resolved upon the path to peace through meditations on the cessation of the waves of the water-like appearances caused by the various conceptualizations of those who have entered the path; yet others, devoid of your grace, did not do so. (99)

When the Blessed One is averse to bestowing grace, even if one has set out upon that difficult path, the atom-like human being attains nothing at all anywhere; for men, there is only the reversal consisting of the five stable stages. 100.

Then, with their shoulders struck by their hands, their brows raised in frowns, and their lips bitten by their teeth, they displayed various kinds of terrible transformations and gestures born of cruel rage.
With eyes slightly reddened, he then shone forth in the assembly. //1//
When such greatness exists in their shoulders, who indeed can be called enemies who would engage in such contradictory conduct? "Oh,
how futile is the bulkiness of these two!"— with this intention, he struck the peaks of the shoulders of the heroes.
Or, throbbing is the agitation caused by an abundance of the itch for battle. //1//
With the surface of the floor trembling under the weight of his placed feet, and with the knot of his spotless crown loosened by the friction [of his movement],
Krodha entered the assembly hall of the Enemy of Smara, the soft hem of his silk garment trailing down as it caught upon the tips of his armlets.

Upon the chest of the enraged Gaṇapati, the thick rows of pearls splashing from the severed necklaces produced a beauty as if sprinkled by a multitude of drops of perspiration from the Goddess of Fortune, who had previously fled and sought refuge at his feet.
Previously, even before the battle had been fought, they fled in fear and took to flight. //3//

Spreading a shadow that darkened the expanse of the sky and the quarters of the horizon, Kālamusala, with a face made terrifying by the manifestation of a frown, seemed to desire to bring about the creation of a night for the destruction of the entire world of his enemies.

The *kālamusala* and other such groups [of deities] are present here. Because she effects the withdrawal of the creation of enemies, she is the "Night of Time" (*kālarātrī*) in this context, owing to her nature as the agent of dissolution. // 4 //
With a mind heavy with wrath born of fury, Vīrabhadra let out a terrifying roar of "huṃ" in battle—
a sound made long by the echoes from within the hollows of the cavernous interior of his gaping mouth, which was wide open in a yawn.
By those [means], namely the fury and the displays of pride directed toward battle in the conflict. //5//
Dense with the sound of *huṃ* uttered without the terrifying restraint of intense, unrestrained fury,
and loud with the noise of striking shoulders, the warriors somehow managed to maintain the connection between heaven and earth.
Bhairavī is connected with Hara; [she is] "of heaven and earth. // 6 //
With his lotus-like hand, Meghanīla angrily tore off and cast away the garland from her neck—
a garland upon which bees were dissolved in the thick, trickling nectar—
as if in a sudden impulse to destroy the playful splendor of the Fortune of the Enemy who had arrived there in the midst of the passion of love.
From the forehead of the Three-formed Lord, who was fiercely enraged in the assembly, a reddish-pale streak [of ash] rose from the temple to his palm;
it appeared above his third eye like a fresh sprout of smoke rising upward.

With his face turned askance, his gaze reddened by a frown that had grown dim, and his arm appearing as if being consumed to ashes by the fire of his own fame— fame whose essence was celebrated for its unrestrained valor— the king was beheld by Śikhi, who was white with the rays of his laughter.
Bearing a face with his adamantine fist held as if trembling from the fear of being bitten by his own teeth, his lower lip quivering and agitated;
he struck his staff-like arm with his hand, while a continuous eruption of horripilation blossomed upon him from the passion of his fury in crushing the enemies of the gods. 10.
The winds of his breath, entering the path of the fissures revealed in the earth by the impact of his hands as he lowered his face,
made the lotus in the depths of the netherworld bear white lotuses as pale as the upraised hoods of Śeṣa.
The lotus pond was indeed within the depths of Pātāla;
when the earth was split open by the impact of Anala’s hand,
the winds from his breath entered through that fissure and rendered it like a white lotus with its remaining petals shaken out by the wind.
Tawny with the thick pollen of the fresh filaments of the flowers in his crest, a bee fell through the intoxication of honey;
it was like the star of the upward eye of Bhṛṅgiriṭi as he suddenly rubbed his forehead, reddish-brown as a flame of fire.
From the cavity of his mouth, Naḍakūbara— his eyes reddened with rage— emitted a mass of smoke from his *huṃkāra* outbursts,
as if out of eagerness to swallow the sovereign of the Daityas whole.
The people gazed upon her as she suddenly leapt up, like a magical spell (kṛtyā). // 13 //
Naḍakūbara is the son of Dhanada, a friend of Hara; he is a specific deity who creates great calamities through his magical powers (kṛtyā). // 13 //

The cluster of bees, languidly dissolved through the confidence of excessive drinking of the makaranda nectar hanging from his neck, shone like a chain of blue-lotus garlands upon the victorious one, who was like an elephant in the lake of battle with his arrogant enemies. 14.
There, the garland of blue lotuses shone like a chain for the victorious one (Arjuna) in his elephant form, as he agitated that lake which was indeed an enemy of the gods. 14.
Considering his own arm— the tree— to be his sole sinless companion in battle, he stroked it with his palm, performing a ritual ablution with the flood of water from the rays of his effortless nails.
Then, his form became difficult to behold, and he caused distress to all the worlds.

The one of beautiful form, whose majesty was undiminished, beheld the orb of the sun— a singular form that was both difficult to look upon and terrifying— wherein the delusion of headless trunks seemed to cling due to the attachment of streaks of wet smoke arising from its friction against the swinging forehead.

*Kaṣaṇa* means tearing asunder. Sumūrti beheld—that is, showed—the solar disc such that it created the illusion that a headless trunk (*kabandha*) was clinging there due to its connection with streaks of smoke;
a *kabandha* is a headless male figure that portends calamity, though others identify it as Rāhu.
His splendor was unassailable, and his beauty was complete. // 16 //
The mass of smoke rising from the hollow of his cupped hands shone as it ascended into the sky through its intense mutual entanglement,
like a row of bees emerging from the interior of the calyx of a white lotus whose petals were slightly unfolded.
The mass of smoke-crested flames is the *carcā* (marking); the two hands joined together form the *karapuṭa*.
And the row of skulls upon the crown of Krodheśvara [is formed] by the touch of the mass of flame-tips from his upward-gazing eyes. // 17 //
The mountain peak, scorched by the rays of the sun at the time of universal dissolution, let out a loud, crashing roar as its summit shattered. // 18 //
The lotus-world of the wrathful Lord Caṇḍeśvara, its stalk— the bodies of the remaining beings— completely agitated, and its broad petals— the massive clouds— whirling about.
She withered under the power of the heat from her intensely hot sighs. // 19 //
The one whose banner is the palm tree trembled, dripping with beads of sweat, his mouth gaping with a terrifying yawn that reddened the surface of his palate;
was this due to the intense embrace of the Fortune of the Enemy standing before him—whom he had conquered through mere thought—or rather, from the force of his fierce passion? (20)

Tālaketu trembled due to the intense passion that served as its cause; this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) suggesting it was as if from a longing for the embrace of Śrī. For one desiring to embrace, perspiration, trembling, and yawning manifest. The word *uta* has the sense of "as if" (*iva*). 20.
The arm of the buffalo-bannered god, whose face was turned sideways, shone like the trunk of a victorious elephant, variegated with the application of ashes white as a flash of laughter.
His broad shoulders were like formidable, high-rising frontal globes upon a pedestal. // 21 //
Thus, at the onset of night, while the eyes of the cakora birds were fixed intently upon their beloveds,
other women reached a state of extreme distress due to separation from their lovers;
those other matrons fell into a precarious condition under the power of their bereavement.
The curved digit of the moon bore the semblance of the staff of the god of love’s bow;
and the rays emanating from it, like arrows impelled by him, caused pain to that slender woman.
(2) "Impelled by him" means driven by Kāma.
At that time, no distinction could be perceived anywhere between darkness and the light of the moon;
for both produced a long-lasting blindness in her during her separation from her fair-limbed beloved.
Since even the lunar light, like darkness, caused such blindness during the separation, no difference was seen between the two for the woman in love.

The wind, born from the feathers of the arrows of the flower-bowed god, fanning the fire of the flames of separation, quickly consumed the hearts of the fair-browed women, which had lost their steadfastness.
Who here, even if faultless, does not turn toward hostility when beset by calamity?

In the absence of Sudṛśā, even the moonbeams, though dripping with nectar, brought the heat of fire to those [women]. (5) Moreover, another woman suffered like a mirror when her heart was clouded by sighs; for, through the dense darkness of her heavy swoon, she perceived the form of her beloved reflected within it. (6)
When the mind is clouded by the darkness of fainting due to labored breaths—as if by a mirror obscured by mist—even another woman’s wife is tormented with grief.
Like a delicate flower violently shaken from its stalk by the southern breeze,
the mind of the girl with curved brows fell away from the abode of the Jina;
as if he, desiring to fashion another string for the bow of Madana, had drawn it back toward the seat of his arrow.
The body, with its skin like a web of lotus fibers, was shaken by the wind from the left eye.
(8) As the union with his beloved was attained, his heart—oppressed by the weight of a heavy burden of anxiety—breathed heavily and deeply, as if overcome by the intensity of its exhaustion. (9)
"Bhara" means a collection.
Abandon your grief; this fever of separation shall soon pass away for you.
Take heart for a moment, for it is possible to dispel misfortune through fortitude.
(10) *Saṃjvara* means intense heat or anguish.
Wandering with sweet warbling out of a longing for the blue lotuses worn long ago,
a bee approached the edge of [her] ear as if to console someone in this way.
Here, anxieties enter without hesitation due to separation from a beloved.
Smara, as if thinking, "The door is wide open," pierced his mind with arrows as if it were wounded. 12.

With the expansive reflections on the love for his beloved, which had remained in an uninterrupted succession, he—his body held in suspense—made his descent into the mind as if into a sacred bathing place (tīrtha). 13.
"Unbroken tradition" refers to those who have remained by acting in such a way that there is a continuous, repeated practice.
"Vimarṣa" means critical inquiry.
"Tīrtha" is a path for descending, serving as a staircase.
*Avatāraḥ* means descending;
here, the formation with the suffix *ghañ* should be considered as occurring in the sense of arising (*utpatti*).
It is also [used for] a lake (*mānasa-saras*).
Bound by a garland of mental constructs consisting of the turbulent recollections of her unfulfilled desires,
the meditation of the fair-browed woman crept after her beloved as if it were exceedingly long.
(14) *Sasṛpe* means it spread forth.

And the pitiless Madana did not cease from placing upon his bowstring the brow of that lady with arched eyebrows—who was in a state of emaciation—nor the string itself, while fixing upon it a flower whose form is as delicate as her own. 15
